summary: Describes how routers that support SR-MPLS and routers that only handle IP can work together. SR-MPLS label stacks are carried across IP-only parts of the network by encapsulation or tunneling, such as MPLS-over-UDP, with no changes to the SR-MPLS specifications.

eli5.summary: Sometimes part of the trip has no special road, so you put the whole travel plan inside a plain box and ship it across. This explains that for routers.

questions: how does mpls over udp carry segment routing
why push explicit null in sr-mpls over udp
subtitle: How SR-MPLS routers can cross IP-only routers by wrapping labeled packets in UDP tunnels.

tldr.problem: SR-MPLS steers packets with a stack of MPLS labels, but some routers on the path may be IP-only and unable to forward labeled packets.
tldr.mechanism: When the next hop cannot handle SR-MPLS, the router pops the top label and wraps the rest of the packet in an IP tunnel, usually MPLS-over-UDP from RFC 7510, addressed to the next SR-MPLS-capable node on the path. That node strips the tunnel header and carries on.
tldr.outcome: SR-MPLS and IP-only routers can coexist, with no changes to the SR-MPLS specifications, and SR-MPLS islands can be joined across a legacy IP network.

facts.label: Node types in an SR-MPLS domain

today: RFC 8663 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7510 and RFC 8660.

sections.title: SR-MPLS Across IP Networks
sections.content:
MPLS Segment Routing (SR-MPLS, RFC 8660) is source routing. The sender imposes a stack of MPLS labels that fully or partly specifies the path and any instructions to carry out along it. Because the instructions are just an MPLS label stack, they can be used across MPLS, IPv4 and IPv6 data planes.

This RFC describes how SR-MPLS-capable routers and IP-only routers can coexist by combining SR-MPLS label stacks with IP encapsulation or tunneling, such as MPLS-over-UDP (RFC 7510). It makes no changes to the SR-MPLS specifications and interworks with existing SR-MPLS implementations.
sections.eli5: A travel plan written as a stack of stickers works on special roads. This RFC says what to do when a stretch of road does not understand stickers.

sections.title: Use Cases for Tunneling
sections.content:
In every case an IP tunnel such as MPLS-over-UDP is used. The tunnel's remote endpoint MUST equal the address of the next SR-MPLS-capable node on the SR path, the egress of the active segment. The source address is an address of the encapsulating node.

  • Incremental deployment: SR-MPLS packets are tunneled across parts of the network that are not SR-MPLS, joining islands of SR-MPLS such as data center sites.
  • Entropy: with MPLS-over-UDP, the UDP source port serves as an entropy field, which helps use Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) and Link Aggregation Groups (LAGs) well. This contrasts with RFC 4023, where MPLS-over-IP has no entropy mechanism.
  • No SRv6 and no MPLS: it enables Segment Routing in an IP network whose routers lack SRv6 support and where MPLS forwarding is not an option.

The RFC notes that using UDP may be particularly beneficial because it is agnostic of the underlying transport.
sections.eli5: You might need the tunnel to join two faraway islands, to spread traffic over many lanes, or because the middle roads only understand plain addresses.

sections.title: Building Forwarding Entries
sections.content:
Take router A holding a packet whose top label is L(E), the label for Prefix-SID SID(E) advertised by router E. If the next hop toward E is IP-only while A and E are both SR-MPLS-capable, A builds its forwarding entry as follows.

  • E advertises its Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB), as defined in RFC 8402. That can be done with IGPs, BGP or configuration protocols.
  • When E advertises SID(E) it MUST also advertise the egress endpoint address and the encapsulation type of any tunnel used to reach E, flooded domain wide. If A and E are in different routing domains, this MUST be flooded into both.
  • A programs the entry for the prefix with either a pop of the top label, or a swap to SID(E) plus the lower bound of E's SRGB, depending on the advertised action.

When forwarding, A encapsulates the packet in the advertised way and sends it toward the next hop. A non-normative example uses OSPF and IS-IS extensions: the choice between pop and swap follows the No-PHP (NP) flag in OSPF or the Persistent (P) flag in IS-IS. A clear flag means pop and a set flag means swap. Where no mechanism negotiates a port, the RFC 7510 ports apply: 6635 for MPLS in UDP and 6636 for MPLS-over-UDP with DTLS.
sections.eli5: Each router tells the others where its special entrance is and how to knock. A router that wants to send something there looks up the entrance and knocks the right way.

sections.title: Forwarding Packets Hop by Hop
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes six kinds of node: the domain ingress, legacy transit nodes (IP-only), SR-MPLS transit nodes not named in the stack, SR-MPLS transit nodes that are named by a SID, the penultimate SR-MPLS-capable node, and the domain egress.

In the worked example with penultimate hop popping (PHP), routers A, E, G and H are SR-MPLS-capable and B, C, D and F are IP-only. A wants to send to H along the path E, G, H. It imposes labels L(G) and L(H), pops the label for E and wraps the packet in a UDP tunnel to E. E strips the tunnel, sees that the next hop toward G is IP-only, and tunnels to G. G reaches the end of the stack, so G pushes an explicit NULL label (RFC 3032) before tunneling to H. Without it the payload, which could be any protocol, would sit under a UDP header as if it were MPLS.

Without PHP, each segment's label stays in place until the end of the segment, then is popped and the next instruction is processed.
sections.eli5: A hands the parcel to a courier going to the next stop that understands the stickers. That stop peels off the wrapper, reads the next sticker, and hires another courier. The last stop adds a note so the parcel is not misread.

sections.title: Extra Forwarding Details
sections.content:
Tunneling also helps when the top label is an Adjacency SID and the adjacent node cannot do MPLS forwarding but can still process SR-MPLS packets. Local policy can also prefer an MPLS-over-UDP tunnel even when the next hop is MPLS-capable.

For the outer IP header, IPv4 or IPv6 may be used. Fields such as ECN, DSCP and IPv6 Flow Label SHOULD be configurable according to operator policy. They may be copied or promoted from the packet, or set from instructions tied to the SID. TTL handling follows RFC 7510.

For entropy, the encapsulator MAY fill the UDP source port with a value that identifies the flow, for example by copying an entropy label or hashing the label stack or the payload's five-tuple. It MAY be desirable to keep the incoming UDP source port value and reuse it on the outgoing tunnel, to avoid recomputing it. On congestion, all considerations of RFC 7510 and RFC 8085 apply, noting that SR-MPLS traffic is likely to be IP traffic.
sections.eli5: The wrapper has its own labels too, and the operator decides how to fill them in. A random-looking number on the wrapper helps spread parcels over many lanes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8354 and RFC 7510 apply, and RFC 8402 provides those for Segment Routing. DTLS (RFC 6347) SHOULD be used where security is needed on an SR-MPLS-over-UDP segment, including when it crosses the public Internet or another untrusted environment.

The RFC argues that it is difficult for an attacker to pass a raw MPLS packet into a network, and operators can exclude packets that carry MPLS as the payload of IP tunnels. A network ingress node can easily detect an attempt to smuggle in an IP packet, because the UDP destination port would be set to MPLS, and such filtering SHOULD be applied. If an IGP is used to advertise other UDP ports, port filtering becomes harder. Any control-plane protocols used must also be adequately secured.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Treat the wrapper like a sealed envelope. Guards at the border can check that outsiders do not slip in envelopes that claim to hold special travel plans, and a lock (DTLS) protects envelopes that cross unsafe territory.
